title: Gross Margin
subtitle: Measuring production efficiency and pricing power
openingQuestion: Apple's Gross Margin is ~45%, Walmart's is ~24%. Is Apple better than Walmart?
openingOptions: They can't be compared - different industries have different cost structures
explanation: Gross margin shows how much is left after subtracting the direct cost of making the product - in other words, the room available to pay for everything else. What counts as good depends entirely on the industry: 45% is healthy for electronics, while 24% is already very good for a supermarket, because it makes up for it with an extremely fast inventory turnover. A low margin isn't bad by itself; a low margin combined with slow turnover is what's bad. That's why comparing across industries almost always leads to the wrong conclusion.

diagram.label: Subtract the direct cost of production
Only meaningful against a peer in the same industry

realWorldExample.description: Apple holds a Gross Margin around 45% thanks to premium pricing and a strong brand in consumer technology, while Walmart runs at about 24% because grocery retail is fiercely price-competitive - both are successful business models in their own way.

quiz.question: Gross margin falls from 40% to 35% over 2 years - what does that suggest?
options: Rising tax, since tax is subtracted directly within cost of goods sold
Falling revenue, since Gross Margin is calculated on absolute revenue
Pricing pressure, rising input costs, or a shift in product mix
Nothing to worry about, a 5-point swing is normal every year
quiz.explanation: A declining gross margin is a warning signal worth investigating: (1) falling pricing power; (2) rising input costs not yet passed on to selling price; (3) higher-margin products being displaced by lower-margin ones.

quiz.question: A retailer has a much lower Gross Margin than a tech company. Does that mean the retailer is running a worse business?
options: Yes, a lower Gross Margin always means a distinctly worse business
The retailer should always switch to a tech model to improve its margin
Gross Margin has no meaning at all when judging the retail industry
No - retail runs a low-margin, high-turnover model and can still deliver a good ROE
quiz.explanation: This is exactly why you can't compare Gross Margin across industries: retail's 'low margin, high turnover' model can produce an ROE equal to or better than the tech industry.

quiz.question: Revenue is 2,000 billion, cost of goods sold is 1,300 billion. What is the Gross Margin?
options: 35% (= (2,000 − 1,300) ÷ 2,000, gross profit over revenue)
65% (= 1,300 ÷ 2,000, taking the cost share)
700 billion (= 2,000 − 1,300, gross profit not yet divided by revenue)
53.8% (= 700 ÷ 1,300, dividing by cost by mistake)
quiz.explanation: Gross Margin = (Revenue − COGS) / Revenue = 700/2,000 = 35%. Every 100 dong of revenue leaves 35 dong to cover selling, admin, interest, and tax.

quiz.question: Gross Margin stays stable but Operating Margin keeps falling over three years. Where does the problem lie?
options: In raw-material input prices rising faster than selling prices
In selling and administrative costs, not cost of goods sold
In rising interest expense from the business taking on new debt
In an increase to the corporate tax rate during the period
quiz.explanation: These two margins differ only in the block of operating costs. If cost of goods stays proportionally the same while the operating margin keeps falling, that means SG&A is growing faster than revenue.

quiz.question: Why is a software company's Gross Margin usually over 70% while a supermarket's is only around 20-25%?
options: Because software companies enjoy larger tax incentives than supermarkets
Because supermarkets have to spend much more on advertising and promotions
Because selling one more copy of software costs almost nothing in production
Because supermarkets turn over inventory many times faster
quiz.explanation: The marginal cost of the millionth software copy is close to zero, while a supermarket has to buy each item before reselling it. Gross margin reflects the cost structure of the model, which is why comparing it across industries is meaningless.

keyTakeaways: Reflects pricing power and production efficiency
Compare within the same industry - each has its own benchmark

practicePrompt.question: A company has Revenue = 800 billion, COGS = 480 billion. What is this company's Gross Margin, and what does that number tell you?
options: Gross Margin = Gross Profit / Revenue = (800-480)/800 = 40% - meaning the company keeps 40 dong of gross profit from every 100 dong of revenue, before subtracting operating costs
Gross Margin = 480/800 = 60%, showing the ratio of production cost to the company's revenue
Gross Margin cannot be calculated without knowing the company's operating costs (SG&A)
Gross Margin = 800-480 = 320 billion, an absolute figure rather than a percentage
practicePrompt.explanation: Gross Margin = Gross Profit / Revenue = (800-480)/800 = 40%. This measures core production/business efficiency - for every 100 dong of revenue, the company keeps 40 dong after subtracting the direct cost of making the product.

summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Reflects pricing power and production efficiency

application.title: Calculate a real Gross Margin
application.message: Open a company's income statement, divide Gross Profit by Revenue, then compare it with a peer in the same industry to see who has stronger pricing power.
application.secondary: Don't compare gross margin across different industries - each industry has its own benchmark.

sections.text: Gross Margin is the first and simplest metric for assessing a business: after subtracting the direct cost of production/purchasing (COGS), what percentage of revenue is left? It reflects two things at once - production efficiency and the business's pricing power.

sections.label: The formula
sections.text: Gross Margin = Gross Profit / Revenue = (Revenue − COGS) / Revenue
Why Apple and Walmart are both 'right' despite a 2x difference in margin

Apple holds a Gross Margin around 45% thanks to a strong brand and premium pricing on consumer technology products - customers are willing to pay more for an iPhone rather than buy a cheaper phone with similar features. Walmart only reaches about 24% because grocery retail is a fiercely price-competitive industry with a low margin on each item. Both are successful business models - Walmart makes up for it with an extremely fast inventory turnover, selling through its stock many times a year.

A company whose Gross Margin falls from 40% to 35% over 2 years is a signal worth investigating right away, even if revenue is still rising. The three most common causes: (1) competitive pressure forcing a lower selling price; (2) rising raw-material cost not yet passed on to selling price; (3) a shifting product mix - higher-margin products selling more slowly, lower-margin products selling more.

items: A high Gross Margin is usually tied to a strong brand, differentiated products, and few direct competitors
A low Gross Margin doesn't mean a worse business - you also need to look at inventory turnover
A margin declining for 2-3 periods in a row is a more important warning signal than one single down quarter
Only compare Gross Margin within the same industry - comparing across industries is nearly meaningless

lines: Gross Margin answers the question of whether a business prices and produces efficiently - but says nothing yet about the operating costs sitting behind it.
